claims.claim: Economic activity is divided into sectors: primary (extraction of raw materials), secondary (manufacturing/industry), tertiary (services), and quaternary (knowledge/information); industry is the secondary sector.

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain around the 1760s and is conventionally dated to roughly 1760-1840; it started in the textile industry and accelerated with the adoption of steam power. The term 'industrial revolution' was popularized by the historian Arnold Toynbee (in 1884).

The Industrial Revolution's decisive geographic change was the factory: production moved from scattered household hand-work to centralized factories, driving rapid urbanization (in England the urban share rose from about 9 percent in 1800 to about 62 percent in 1900).

Alfred Weber (1868-1958) published a least-cost theory of industrial location in 1909, holding that profit-seeking firms locate at the lowest-total-cost site, shaped by three factors: transport costs (the most important), labor costs, and agglomeration.

In Weber's model, transport cost rises with weight and distance, so bulk-reducing industries (whose output weighs less than their inputs, e.g., smelters, lumber mills) locate near the raw material, while bulk-gaining industries (whose output is heavier/bulkier) locate near the market; agglomeration and deagglomeration are secondary considerations.

Fordism is standardized mass production credited to Henry Ford's assembly line (specialize/simplify jobs, standardize parts, high wages), which drove twentieth-century manufacturing growth; post-Fordism (flexible production) took hold from about the 1980s, relocating production components across many places and countries and assembling them elsewhere.

A global shift moved manufacturing from older industrial regions toward newly industrialized countries; as wages rose in earlier NICs, some production shifted onward (e.g., from China toward Vietnam and Indonesia), while older industrial regions experienced deindustrialization, with manufacturing income in long-industrialized economies reckoned to have peaked around 1965-1975.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The precise dating of the Industrial Revolution.
positions: The World History Encyclopedia dates the British Industrial Revolution to 1760-1840 and notes Arnold Toynbee coined/popularized the term in 1884.
Dastrup's OER describes England as already among the wealthiest nations 'by 1750' and locates the key innovations in the 'late 18th century,' without a single start year.
Historians agree the process was gradual rather than a single event, so exact boundary years vary by source.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the Industrial Revolution 'began in Britain around the 1760s' and is 'conventionally dated to roughly 1760 to 1840,' language that both sources support, and notes the term was popularized by Toynbee, avoiding false precision about a single start date.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Weber is the sole originator of industrial-location thinking.
positions: Weber (1909) is standardly credited with the least-cost model.
Some OER trace antecedents to von Thunen and other German location theorists; one source garbles a predecessor's name.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the least-cost model and the three factors to Weber (dated 1909) without claiming he invented all location theory, and does not reproduce the garbled predecessor name found in one source.
